content: Kernicterus is a rare but severe neurological condition that can develop in newborns with extreme jaundice. It is also referred to as bilirubin encephalopathy. The symptoms of kernicterus vary depending on its stage: Early stage symptoms include intense jaundice, absence of the startle reflex, difficulty feeding or sucking, and profound lethargy. Mid-stage symptoms may involve a high-pitched cry, an arched back with the neck hyperextended backward, a bulging fontanel (the soft spot on a baby’s head), and seizures. Late-stage symptoms, which represent the full neurological syndrome, include high-frequency hearing loss, intellectual disability, muscle rigidity, speech difficulties, seizures, and movement disorders. The underlying cause of kernicterus is excessively high levels of bilirubin in the blood. Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced during the normal breakdown of red blood cells. When bilirubin levels become critically elevated, it can cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit in brain tissue, leading to severe neurological damage. This condition typically develops within the first week of life but can occasionally occur up to the third week. Newborns with hemolytic diseases, such as Rh hemolytic disease, are at particularly high risk for severe jaundice and kernicterus. However, kernicterus can also occur in otherwise healthy infants. Immediate medical attention is necessary if a baby shows any signs of kernicterus. Diagnosis is confirmed through blood tests that reveal dangerously high bilirubin levels, typically exceeding 20-25 mg/dL. It is important to note that normal bilirubin ranges may vary slightly between laboratories, so results should be interpreted by a healthcare provider. Treatment for kernicterus depends on the infant’s age in hours and the presence of any risk factors, such as prematurity. Common treatments include phototherapy (light therapy) to lower bilirubin levels and exchange transfusions in severe cases. The prognosis for kernicterus is serious, and the condition often has a guarded outcome. Many infants with advanced neurological complications do not survive. Potential complications include permanent brain damage, hearing loss, and death. Preventing kernicterus involves early detection and management of jaundice or any underlying conditions that contribute to elevated bilirubin levels. If bilirubin levels are high, the infant should be evaluated for hemolytic diseases. Additionally, all newborns should have a follow-up appointment within 2 to 3 days after hospital discharge, especially if they are premature or near-term.
